Author: Cryptlex
Highlights:
When a machine has no internet access at the time of activation, your app cannot reach the Cryptlex servers directly. Instead, you activate the license offline by exchanging files through the admin or customer portal.
...
1. Your app generates a request file. The user enters their license key, and LexActivator writes an offline activation request file that identifies the license and the machine.
2. The request is exchanged for a response. You (or your customer) upload the request file on the admin or customer portal from any machine that has internet access, such as a phone, laptop, or edge device. The portal validates it and returns an offline activation response file that is valid for a limited period.
3. Your app consumes the response. LexActivator reads the response file to activate the license on the offline machine and stores the activation on disk in encrypted form.

Once activated, your app verifies the license locally on every start, with no internet access required. For a time-bound license, LexActivator returns the `LA_EXPIRED` status when the license expires, which your application should handle based on your business requirements.

 While the machine has no connection, nothing you change on the license reaches it. Renewals, suspension or revocation, entitlement changes, and updated metadata all apply only once the machine completes a server sync or consumes a fresh offline activation response. Take that into account before relying on remote changes to an offline license.
...
Take the request file to any machine with internet access. In the admin portal, open the `Activations` page, click `CREATE OFFLINE`, upload the offline activation request file, set the validity of the response file, and click `ACTIVATE`. If the request is valid, the offline activation response file can be downloaded.

The response file is valid only for the period you set, so it must be consumed on the offline machine before that period expires. On the admin portal you can configure this validity; on the customer portal it is fixed at 3 days.

Response validity is not the same as the license's expiration date. The expiration date is set on the license itself and enforced after activation as usual. Keep the response validity as short as your delivery workflow allows, since the file stays consumable on that machine for the full window.

 An expired response file cannot be revived. If the validity period lapses before the offline machine consumes it, generate a new offline activation request on that machine and exchange it for a fresh response. 

 Your customers can also log in to the customer portal and download the response file themselves, which saves you time on product support. This is useful when the offline machine is isolated but the customer has internet access on another device.
...
Besides the portals, you can generate the response programmatically through the `POST /v3/activations/offline-activate` endpoint, which is useful for building your own tooling, such as an internal utility a service engineer runs on a connected laptop. The request body takes the `licenseId`, the content of the offline activation request file as `offlineRequest`, and the `responseValidity` in seconds. The endpoint identifies the license by `licenseId`, not by its key; if your tooling only has the license key, resolve the ID first with a `GET /v3/licenses?key= ` lookup.

 The endpoint requires a Web API access token. Never embed the token in an application you ship to customers; call the endpoint from your own backend or an internal tool instead. See personal access tokens.

Keygen Relay helps you securely distribute node-locked licenses in offline and air-gapped customer environments, backed by Keygen Cloud or a self-hosted instance of Keygen.
...
Relay, in it's simplest form, is a small server that sits on a local network, which has a pool of licenses — a license file and license key pair — to distribute to nodes on a first-come, first-served basis. Relay provides a vendor-facing CLI for management, as well as an app-facing REST API that allows nodes to claim a lease on a license and release it when no longer needed.

Relay is built on top of Keygen's concept of license files, which are a cryptographically signed and encrypted snapshot of a license object. As such, they are tamper-proof, and a powerful building block for any offline licensing solution.

Relay is not a drop-in replacement for Keygen Cloud or a self-hosted instance of Keygen. It is built on top of Keygen's concept of "license files", offering a small API for managing license leases on behalf of nodes in a local network.

In low-trust environments, Relay itself can be node-locked.
...
Relay was developed to solve a problem in cloud-based licensing APIs: implementing node-based licensing models, such as floating licenses, in air-gapped or offline environments. These environments pose challenges since external licensing APIs require an internet connection, preventing nodes from communicating with the API, making it difficult to track activations or assert node limits in an automated way.
